<reason>CON (Side A) won because it made the debate decidable. PRO's case rested on a motive theory (loans as self-insurance, re-election as "choosing among remnants," NGEU as confession) that CON persuasively characterized as reclassifying every act of giving as hierarchy. When PRO pressed the fair question of what evidence short of exit CON would accept, CON answered directly with five concrete falsifiable outcomes, blunting PRO's later "that test cannot lose" charge. CON also exploited two PRO concessions—"both votes counted" on Greece, and "Italian spreads" as a motive for 2018 forbearance—turning the latter into "worrying about Rome while restructuring Athens is shared fate." PRO's strongest live point, that political distrust can deepen while exit remains ruinous and euro support coexists with collapsing trust in fairness, was real and never fully dissolved, but PRO offered mostly assertion and repeated the "coexistence is the wound" line rather than building out evidence of the depth of distrust. CON's Rebuttal 2 was clipped, a modest execution cost, but the margin stays clear because CON adapted across rounds and narrowed the clash to conduct versus stories, while PRO largely restated its frame.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The 2018 maturity exchange: CON's Q2 forced PRO to name a self-interest for post-contagion forbearance; PRO's A2 offered "official claims" plus "Italian spreads," and CON's A4.3–A4.4 turned the Italian-spreads answer into an admission of shared fate, converting PRO's own explanation into evidence for CON.</best_rebuttal>
